title: How To Handle Disrespectful Students Who Don't Know They're Being Disrespectful dont-know-theyre-being-disrespectful/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses the tricky case of students whose tone or body language crosses into disrespect without any apparent malicious intent, using two brief classroom examples. He lays out a seven-step process for handling this situation with sensitivity rather than a standard consequence: move on in the moment, pull the student aside about 30 minutes later, avoid confrontation, recount the exact words and actions, model the respectful alternative, pause for a possible apology, and finish with a promise that a repeat will bring a real consequence. He explains that enforcing consequences for behavior a student genuinely doesn't understand to be wrong damages trust and increases resentment. The piece closes by connecting the strategy to the importance of thoroughly teaching respect expectations early in the year, noting that body language and tone are the tell for whether an incident needs immediate correction or gentle instruction.
points: Distinguish between intentional disrespect and unintentional disrespect using a student's tone of voice and body language.
Handle unintentional disrespect with a private, non-confrontational pull-aside conversation about 30 minutes after the incident, not an immediate consequence.
Model the respectful alternative directly for the student so expectations are unmistakably clear.
End the conversation with a promise that a repeat incident will bring an actual consequence.
Teach respect expectations explicitly and early in the year to prevent recurring confusion about where the line is.
quotes: What follows are seven steps that will allow you to handle this surprisingly common situation with grace and sensitivity, while all but removing the chances of it happening again.
Here at SCM we typically don’t recommend private meetings with students regarding their behavior. In this case, however, it’s warranted.
Recount the exact actions and words the student used that triggered your instinct that their behavior was disrespectful. Then simply inform them that it crossed the line.
Finish your conversation with a promise that if it happens again, you’ll enforce a consequence.
And enforcing consequences for behavior your students don’t understand to be wrong will jeopardize your relationship with them.
The good news is that body language and tone of voice will always tell you whether to enforce a consequence immediately or pull the student aside for a brief lesson.
